note: Shared by the Python RuleClassifier and (Phase 2c) a JS browser extension. Patterns use only syntax valid in both engines: no named groups, no variable-length lookbehind, no possessive quantifiers. Matching is per-sentence, so `.` never needs to cross a newline.
severity_note: Applied ACROSS sentences to pick the most restrictive label. Clearance ranks highest because it is the narrowest pool (it implies citizenship plus an active clearance); citizen-only is narrower than US-person, which also admits green-card holders, refugees and asylees.
supersedes_note: Applied WITHIN one sentence. 'Must be a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident' matches both rules, but listing permanent residents means the posting is not citizen-only, so US_PERSON wins regardless of severity.

protect_suffix_patterns.note: U.S. / U.S.C. / i.e. / e.g. / Ph.D. -- a run of single letters each followed by a period, preceded by a non-letter. The non-letter prefix is what stops it matching the final 'e.' of 'experience.'
Common abbreviations. Case-sensitive so a sentence ending in 'no.' or 'St.' at the start of a word is not over-protected.
Numbered list markers and statute numbers: '8.' , '1157.'

negations_note: Sentence-local: a negation only suppresses labels in the sentence it matched. `suppresses_rules` additionally cancels named rules -- the bare 'clearance is mentioned' UNCLEAR rules would otherwise survive a negation and turn 'No security clearance required.' into UNCLEAR instead of OPEN.

rules.note: 'an active security clearance is required', 'Secret Clearance Required', 'Clearance required:'. 'required' must follow the clearance directly: the old 40-character gap read 'clearance eligibility may be required', 'clearance, as required' and 'clearance; U.S. citizenship required' as clearance requirements. 'required by the customer / for the program' is conditional and left to the weaker rules.
rules.label: RESTRICTED_CLEARANCE

rules.note: 'active Secret clearance', 'active U.S. Secret security clearance', 'Active U.S. Secret or TS clearance'. rules.note: 'Eligible to obtain and maintain an active U.S. Secret security clearance', 'must be able to obtain a clearance', 'eligible for a security clearance'. Was UNCLEAR until version 3: it states no clearance held today, but a clearance is only granted to U.S. citizens, so for anyone else the line is a bar. Still UNCLEAR, through the bare clearance-mention rule, when the clearance is conditional ('... if required by the program', 'may be required') or only preferred ('ability to obtain a clearance desired').

The plain requirement to be 'authorized to work in the United States' is not matched at all since version 4: anyone with a work permit meets it, so it restricts nobody and the posting is OPEN unless something else in it says otherwise.

open_signals_note: Found ANYWHERE in the posting (unlike negations, which are sentence-local). A restriction plus a conflicting open signal means the posting contradicts itself, which is UNCLEAR -- a human has to read it.
unless_note: Optional on any pattern: if `unless` also matches the sentence, the pattern does not fire. Used to stop a negated phrase reading as its opposite ('no sponsorship is offered' is not 'sponsorship is offered').
